blocks.text: Following the completion of the temple and royal palace, God appears to Solomon a second time, as he had at Gibeon. This appearance centers on the temple's sacred function: God has hallowed it as a dwelling place for his name, and promises that his eyes and heart will remain there perpetually. The narrative frames the temple not as an automatic guarantee of divine favor, but as a house where prayer will be heard. The temple's holiness is real, but it depends on active divine presence and responsiveness to intercession.

The promise of an enduring throne is conditional on Solomon and his descendants maintaining covenant faithfulness: walking before God with integrity, keeping his commandments and statutes. The warning that follows is stark. If Israel turns to foreign gods, God will cut off Israel from the land, cast out the hallowed temple, and make both land and temple a proverb among all peoples. Even the temple's grandeur will become a sign of judgment. This reversal makes clear that architectural splendor and dynastic promise offer no immunity from divine judgment. Covenant faithfulness is the sole foundation.
